sentences.text: Good summer been going?
This meeting is being recorded.
Yeah, good actually.
Good.
It's.
Well, I mean it's, it's a slight pain in the neck at the same time.
It's nice to have the kids around, but yeah, not too bad.
How about yourself?
Good.
I mean my kids are a little older than yours, so they're, they're, they're flown out of the, out of the nest, so to speak.
So just it's of kind going by quick.
It's like, what are we, like a month into summer already?
Middle, middle later, middle late July.
Summer just kind of creeps up on you.
But yeah, going well.
Like I, you know, knock on wood, no complaints.
Things are busy taking, taking time to enjoy the summer but also moving a lot of projects forward.
So.
Yeah, I've seen you being busy.
I love your email that you sent out.
They look really cool.
Oh, the newsletter you mean?
Yeah, the pri.
The View from Private Equity.
Yeah, I've had.
He's.
Luke is someone I spoke to.
I've spoken of four other people in similar roles in private equity that have invested in the events industry.
One of them, unfortunately, you know, they've got a very strict communications policy at their firm.
He basically after the interview he's like, sorry, but you know, our, our PR team really won't let me release it.
But the other three, it have been really interesting and I'll be doing more of those profiles over the next month or so.
Really interesting to get their take on the space, you know, because they don't have any passion for events or agencies or whatever per se.
You know, they don't live in the space.
They just compare it as an investment.
They could invest in, you know, transistors or, you know, frozen orange juice for all they know.

And they just, you know, comparing, you know, ROI and so to get, you know, the, the structural tailwinds in the industry is really interesting and you know, fairly encouraging I think, you know, particularly given just some of the negative geopolitical and economic headwinds that are, that have popped up over the last couple of months.
Glad, glad you found it interesting.
Appreciate it.
You know, you know, you write these things, you never know who's going to read them, what people are going to say.
I mean, I know the open rates are really good and you know, I could see people clicking on them.
But you know, when I talk to people I get encouraging comments like what you just said.
So appreciate it.
Thank you for, for sharing that.
How's the, How's Capital A doing with and agencies Dot com?
How's your.
How's business these days for you?
Yeah, not too bad.
Not too bad at all.
We've got about three deals closing.
We've been, I guess we've been in the final stages for about four or five agencies for about three or four months.
So yeah, we've finally got signed Lois, and we're doing due diligence for these, for these businesses, which is, which is really good.
And then for Deal Engines, which I probably talked you through last time, but Deal Engines is a business that we bought and rebranded and repositioned is going great guns.
We've got about 30 clients going through there, which has been really good.
It's keeping the team busy, but it's all buy side, deal flow.
So yeah, it's just, it's really good.
It's.
It's kind of like a SaaS business that is sitting underneath all the M and A advisory stuff that we do.
It just kind of churns money through it like a sausage machine.
So.
So yeah, it's been really good.
It kind of really turned a corner about two months ago and started stacking up lots of.
Is that the, like the listing service?
It's sort of like an.
Is that the M and A Marketplace product?
That's Agencies Co.
So that's, that's completely different.
That's sell side.
No, Deal Engines is all buy side deal flow for like other M and A advisories or private equity firms.
Yeah, we do all of the sourcing for the deals, off market deals.
And.
Just plug it into their systems basically.
So yeah, it's going really, really well.
We're super busy.
Nice, nice.
How do you keep track of it all?
You got like three or four companies you're running?
Well, I mean it's not three or four companies, it's the same company, but they're kind of three or four business lines, I guess.
Yeah, I mean it's always been the same business.
I guess we've just strengthened the packaging for each one.
So instead of just being an M and A advisory, we've got a front end and a shop front that brings in new clients all the time, which is good for each of the different things that we do.
So yeah, it's kind of, it's not really changed, but it just is more productized, I guess so that it feels like a.
Something that people can take down off the shelf and, and buy and get on with.
Yeah, I hear you.
Well, appreciate you following up with me and sorry for my turn to drop the ball and getting back to you just the last Month was a little, a little hectic.
I did a few travel, a few trips and it's been catching up with a bunch of projects.

But just, you know, I got the, the, the email trails out in front of me in terms of the, you know, the roll up opportunity and just, you know, hopefully this will be the last call where I can get, get clarity on everything and you know, we can, you know, decide to go or no go.
But do appreciate your, your patience on this.
So just circling back, it seems like if I'm getting my numbers right, that what, you know, my role would be enrolled to bring the, the target agencies together.
Right.
That, that's really the, you know, the key value proposition that you would see for me is the ability to source the companies that would fold into the roll up.
Right.
And you mentioned you have someone, John Simon does the integration work and really just kind of bring them in, keep them in.
Right.

And you know, continue to nurture their involvement, talk them off the ledge if they have, you know, cold feet and just, you know, support John's, John's work on the integration side from the relationship management standpoint with the agencies.
Yeah, that, is that a fair.
That'S the job.
Okay.

So it's sort of like sourcing and then sort of like account management, you know, for lack of a better term, you know, keeping, keeping everybody, keeping the trains on track through the process, so to speak.
Yeah.
How long is that process typically run?

Once, once an agency is in place, and I guess it's a two part question that does the integration process not start until all of the place the players are in place or does it start once you've got like two or three and then it just continues as they get bolted on.
Yeah.

So really from the day that they're onboarded onto the bench, basically then we would start the process of trying to figure out what it is that they do, what they've got, what their back end looks like, what their processes are, what their IP looks like.
It's really a deep.

As the bench deepens, there is more of sort of comparison work between all of those agencies and what, you know, what the duplication looks like, what the teams look like, who wants to stay, who wants to go.
All of that kind of work then obviously then starts to get compared across the whole group.
But yeah, I mean, as soon as somebody is in, then John is starting the work.
Okay, and how long is the onboarding process for each, each time a new agency comes in?
Well, it varies.
I mean it shouldn't really take more than A couple of weeks.
But it really does depend on how good they are at feeding back requests for document.
So the onboarding itself is relatively quick.
Yeah.
And so from when the first agency comes in to when the last one is onboarded, what is that, like six months roughly?
I'm just guessing.
Not necessarily.
I mean once you've got, I guess all of them take three or four months to get going and then once you get that first domino tipped, then everybody comes on a lot more easily as leverage.
Sometimes there's pauses for various reasons, you know, people are away or they, they don't have a handle on their finances until the year end or, and that's a month away or two months away.
So things do start to drag on a little bit for loads of different reasons.
So typically, yeah, it's not really a six month from start to finish necessarily, but every, every sort of roll up is different, you know, and can take different amounts of time.
So trying to gauge the commitment for, for me, in terms of keeping everybody.

Yeah, so, so, yes, so the first part of it, John, is, sorry, is how it is for us to find them and bring them in and they obviously need a lot of front end work to get through that, that process and then once they are sold into the process, then it is a shorter period of time then to get the whole group through.

So in terms of like total commitment, it could look more like 12 to 18 months from, from start to finish, the first three or four months binding, bringing them in obviously then we've got to close them, onboard them and then finish the group.
Once we've got the first couple in, I mean, like I said, it's the first couple of dominoes get tipped and then it becomes a lot easier to start closing other companies into the group.
I mean, just one of the groups that we're working on at the moment.
So the strategy really is to get businesses over one million ebitda, but not necessarily over two million.
But now we've got like the first three.
The next company looks like they're going to be two and a half million ebitda and we have another company that has four and a half million EBITDA that's interested coming in and they take.
Those two companies and then you're basically done.
Well, yeah, but with the other three as well, it gets us up to like nine and a half million.
We're like touching the sides on 10.
So we definitely do a 10x with that group and the large agency is not really interested in the huge amount of upside.
But for Them, it's still like an extra.
No.
You know, just without even exaggerating what the results might look like, it looks like another 15 million for them just to be involved, even knowing that they're bringing most of the heft.
Yeah.
With them.
So for them, they're like, well, we're going to exit anyway, we might as well do it as part of the group if it's a good match for us, etc.
So.
But these guys don't want to come in until the end of August.
So even though we've got three on one that's slightly larger, that will double us in size and then the final one, it still is a process of, you know, tipping the first domino and then moving forward.
Okay.
So from start to finish, the whole process, a year, year and a half, roughly.
Right.
Yeah.
So the majority of work will come up front when we close them.
Obviously there is just a small lump of cash, but there's a bit of cash for your troubles.
But really what we're, what we need to do is keep the wheels on while we finish closing the business and then the capital a side of things can take it to market.

Once we've got all of the, the sort of the map built for, for the integration, we can just go to market as soon as we've got enough ebitda, add more agencies through that initial period of two or three months while we're building the marketing materials and doing our own internal due diligence.
But then the whole, the whole marketing process is another, you know, sort of three to nine months, usually somewhere around there.
I mean, if everything goes nicely, it can be a lot shorter.
But, but yeah, so like to, to, to, to not over egg what it would look like.
I would say it's 12.
It's 12 to 18 months, something like that.
And over that time frame, the fee structure that, that I'd be looking at.

So if I bring these agencies to the table and then your team takes care of the integration and bringing it to market, you're looking, I'd be looking at, correct me if, if I've got it wrong, 15% of the onboarding fees from the agency or 15% of your carry on those.
On those agencies.
Is that right?
So 15% of the, the onboarding fee and, and 15% of the carry.
So both of them.
Okay.
Yeah.
Although one might be deductible from the other, it really does depend how because every single agreement we get could be different.
You know, everybody's negotiating their own points that nobody's coming in and Saying I love that cookie cutter.
I, I want to be, I want to be part of that, that everybody's negotiating.
Right.
Okay.
Okay.
But essentially it would be both.
Yeah.
You get 50% of the cash up front.
That's a small retainer to keep everybody aligned while we just get the work done.
And then obviously there could be another six to 12 months of, you know, process and closing the deal up.
Okay.
And the carry is basically the difference between the valuation of the agencies when they're initially brought in and the valuation of the, you know, combined entity when it's sold.
Less, you know, some expenses.
Yeah, yeah.
So it would look, if we could double the value, it looked like 10 of, of the whole deal.
Yeah.
You know, there is no guarantee of that.
If it was an extra 4x, an extra 3x which we could, we could still do the deals at, it would be more like 6% or something of the whole deal.
Okay.
And is this, is this for a virtual roll up or is the roll up actually going to get executed and then brought to market?
So it is in, in theory or in practice is.
It's a virtual roll up.
However, again, this stuff could change depending on what the interest and who the interest is from.
Yeah.
Did the.
How big of an integration risk is our buyers concerned about if it's a virtual rollout?

You know, if you're saying, hey, we've done the plan, we've mapped out the integration of the tech stack and the staff and here's the new leadership team's going to look like and here's our sales and marketing playbook.
You know, we've kind of, here's the roadmap for running or the blueprint for the combined entities.

The one of the comments that I got from a couple of potential investors, I kind of was bouncing this idea generically off of them is some thought it was really interesting and a couple others said there'd be a significant integration risk.
That just putting it on paper is one thing, actually getting it done is another.
And I've been through a couple of acquisitions where the buyer basically shit the bed with companies they bought of mine.
So I understand where they're coming from.
Yeah, sure.
How you've handled that or if that's come across at all well.

So what we are seeing is, and the deals that we've worked on on the sales side where private equity are buying these rollouts because they have a thesis in that vertical, they don't really understand the depth of how marketing agencies can and can't fit together.
What we're doing, particularly with the expertise of somebody like John is, is to mitigate those concerns that may appear with some.
So not all, some private equity firms are just looking at these and admittedly not, not every single one that we've seen is marketing agencies.
They've been in other different verticals as well, but they're, they're looking at these deals and just seeing the work done.
So we're actually going like 10 steps further than that by, by mapping out the, the integration for them and actually identifying where the risks are.
You know, the stuff that we can see that needs to be done is, is we are mitigating against a lot of those concerns.
It's not going to be for everybody.

I mean there are going to be particularly, I would guess if somebody has very deep knowledge of the marketing, you know, marketing services, private equity space, and they've done a ton of deals, it's probably not going to be for them because they can do the work themselves.
This is more for private equity companies that are wanting to get into this space and they want to accelerate into it as quickly as possible.
So if it is that, and then of course investors and strategic buyers as well who don't mind doing the work, but they can see that they can accelerate from where they are by having a bunch of deals.
And also there is nothing particularly that's going to replace time.
You know, if you just let's say we had 10 agencies that there is no chance that they're just going to integrate all of those on day one.
They'll take the largest two.
Most likely they'll take the largest two, integrate those first and then start bringing in the smaller agencies over a period of time.
So it would still be perhaps like two years of their work before they could start looking at organic growth and then exiting the business.
Right.

But they would have to do nothing else in terms of going out and trying to find those businesses during that next three period, which is where a lot of private equity struggles, particularly in marketing services.
Because they have to, they have to basically get the CEO of the biggest agency to go out and do all of the M and A work.
Pretty much, yeah.
So this mitigates some of that, but yeah, it's not going to be for everybody.
So we have to find the right buyers there for this.

So as I'm.

Exactly.

Sorry, like yourself and like set Heather and, and us, because we're doing this all the time in terms of deal flow instead of doing this deal flow for them.

So it does compress their timeline.

Can they get paid on that?

But yeah, they are just setting up a new fund, buying the acquisitions from the previous one.
They've not been able to exit into.
This, like borrowing from Peter to pay Paul.
It's like, it's like a shelf.

So somebody, somebody's going to get caught out.
Yeah, that, that feels like.
I don't know, I don't know how that gets.

But yeah, interesting.

So this, this helps with a lot of that because instead of having to do you well or sitting on a fund for like, you know, in the seventh, eighth year and they still haven't done with it, which is quite typical.
We give them something that is ready rolls, they can jump in, they do the clipboard work that they're good at, and they can smash it out in a couple of years and exit the fund in time.
So.

Likewise.

- Howard will manage relationships and sourcing for target agencies in the roll-up strategy, collaborating with John Simon on technical integration.

- Andy outlined integration risks, which are being addressed through a detailed mapping process and John's expertise in risk mitigation.  
- Target buyers are identified as private equity firms seeking quick entry into marketing services, along with strategic buyers looking for acceleration.  
- The focus on experiential marketing identifies 1-3 million EBITDA, with an emphasis on founder-led agencies that lack M&A experience.
summary.short_summary: Howard's newsletter 'View from Private Equity' received commendations from Andy for its insights into private equity professionals in the events sector. Capital A has successfully closed three M&A deals, demonstrating robust performance in its Deal Engines business, which now serves 30 clients. In the roll-up strategy, Howard will oversee relationships and sourcing for target agencies while collaborating with John Simon on technical integration, expected to take 12-18 months for new agencies, with onboarding varying between 2-3 weeks based on readiness. A current roll-up example highlights three agencies with a combined projected EBITDA of $9.5 million, aiming to attract larger agencies by the end of August. Howard's compensation includes 15% of onboarding fees and performance-based carry fees, estimated at 6-10% of deal value. Integration risks are being addressed through careful mapping and John's expertise. Target buyers comprise private equity and strategic firms looking to enter the marketing services quickly.
